Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 106, verse 1:

Page 238

Surat Quraysh

It is also said: Surat li-Ilaf Quraysh. It is Meccan according to the majority, and Madani according to al-Dahhak and Ibn al-Sa'ib. Its verses number five according to the Hijazi reckoning and four according to others. Its connection to what precedes it is too clear to be hidden. Indeed, a group said that the two are a single surah, and they argued for this by the fact that Ubayy ibn Ka'b did not separate them with the basmala in his codex, based on what is reported from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Azdi, who said: "I prayed the Maghrib prayer behind 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and in the first rak'ah he recited Wa al-Tin, and in the second Alam tara and li-Ilafi Quraysh, without separating them with the basmala."

It has been answered that a group affirmed the separation in the codex of Ubayy, and the affirming report takes precedence over the negating one. And also: if the report of Ibn Maymun is sound, it allows the possibility that he did not hear it, and perhaps he recited it silently. What indicates that it is an independent surah is what al-Bukhari recorded in his Tarikh, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Khilafiyyat, from Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted favoured Quraysh with seven qualities that no one before them was given and no one after them will be given: that I am among them; and in another wording: prophethood is among them, the caliphate is among them, the custody (of the Ka'bah) is among them, the provision of water is among them, they were victorious over the Elephant, and they worshipped Allah the Exalted for seven years; and in another wording, ten years, during which no one other than them worshipped Him, and a surah of the Qur'an was revealed concerning them in which no one other than them is mentioned: li-Ilafi Quraysh."

Something similar to this last report has come in two other reports: one from al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the second from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from him (ﷺ).

Supporting independence is that its verses are not in the pattern of the verses before it. You know that once the consecutive transmission of the separation is established, there is no need for anything of what has been mentioned.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾. Al-Ilaf, according to what al-Khafaji said, is a verbal noun of aliftu al-shay' and a'lantuhu, from al-Ilf, which, as al-Raghib said, is gathering together with harmony. Al-Harawi said in al-Gharibayn: al-Ilaf refers to the covenants between them and the kings. Hashim used to make a pact with the king of Syria, al-Muttalib with Kisra, and 'Abd Shams and Nawfal with the king of Egypt and Abyssinia. He said: the meaning of yu'alifu is yu'ahidu (makes a covenant) and yusalihu (makes peace). Its verb is ālafa on the pattern of fā'ala, and its verbal noun is ilāf without a yā', on the pattern of qibāl, or alafa of the triliteral, like kataba kitaban. The verb may also come from it on the pattern of af'ala, like amana, and its verbal noun is iylaf, like iman. Interpreting al-Ilaf as covenants is contrary to what the majority hold, as is not hidden from one who investigates. In al-Bahr: iylaf is the verbal noun of ālafa (quadriliteral), and ilaf is the verbal noun of alifa (triliteral). It is said: alifa al-rajul al-amr, alfan and ālafan; and ālafa, when used by another with respect to it, may come transitively with one object, like alifa, and from it is his saying:

Among the sand-dwelling beloved ones, a noble white-necked doe, on whose neck the rays of the morning sun shine.

The readings concerning this will come, God willing. Quraysh are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, and this is the most sound and most established view according to al-Qurtubi. It is said that the jurists hold this view, due to the apparent meaning of what is reported: that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked, "Who is Quraysh?" and he said, "From the descendants of al-Nadr."

It is also said: the descendants of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr. This is reported from the majority. Indeed, al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: the genealogists among Quraysh and others agreed that Quraysh only split off from Fihr, whose name, according to more than one, is Quraysh, with Fihr being his epithet, and he is known by the kunya Abu Ghalib. It is also said: the descendants of Mukhallad ibn al-Nadr, and this is weak.

In some biographies it is said that al-Nadr ibn Kinanah has no progeny except Malik, and this is even weaker. Rather, it is a Rafidi statement, intending by it to deny the rightfulness of the caliphate of the two Shaykhs. (It is also said) that they are the descendants of Qusayy ibn Kilab. It is also said: 'Urwah, famous by his epithet Kilab, for his abundant hunting, or for his mukalabah, i.e., his pursuing of enemies in war. Yes, Qusayy gathered Quraysh in the Haram until they took it as a dwelling, after they had been scattered elsewhere, and this is what the poet meant by his saying:

Page 239

Our father Qusayy was called "the Gatherer"; through him Allah gathered the tribes from Fihr.

It therefore does not indicate at all what he claimed. Originally, Quraysh is the diminutive of qarsh, with the qaf vowelled with fatha, a name for a sea creature, the strongest of its animals: it eats and is not eaten, and it dominates and is not dominated. Ibn 'Abbas answered Mu'awiyah with this when he asked him, "Why was Quraysh named Quraysh?" That creature is called qarsh, as is mentioned in the words of the scholar, and it is also called Quraysh. Upon this is the verse of Tubba', as related by Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi, and the scholar also recited it for Mu'awiyah, except that he attributed it to al-Jumahi:

Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea, and by them Quraysh was named Quraysh.
They eat the fat and the lean and never leave, on any day, a feather to the one with two wings.
Thus in the lands the tribe of Quraysh eats up the lands in a comprehensive consumption.
And at the end of time they will have a prophet who will greatly slay among them and wound them.

Al-Farra' said: it is from taqarrush, meaning earning a livelihood; they were named so for their trade. It is also said it is from taqrish, which means searching, and from it is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

O mocking one who searches out our affairs before 'Amr, is there any remaining for us?

They were named so because their forefather used to search out those with needs in order to fulfil their needs, and likewise they would search out the needy among the pilgrims in order to meet them. It is also said: from taqarrush, which means gathering together, and from it is his saying:

Brothers who gathered the sins against us, in tales of their time and of old.

They were named so for gathering together after dispersal. The diminutive, when the word is from a derived form, is a diminutive of tarkhim (abbreviation); when it is from a triliteral root without additions, it stays on its original pattern. In either case it is for glorification, as in his saying:

And every people, there will come between them a great calamity from which the fingertips turn yellow.

The relative adjective is Qurashi and Qurayshi, as in the Qamus. They agreed to its being diptote here, considering in it the meaning of the tribe. It is permissible to treat it as non-diptote, considering in it the meaning of the group, due to its being a proper noun and feminine, and on this is his saying:

And Quraysh sufficed for the difficult matters and was their lord.

From Sibawayh, he said regarding words like Ma'add, Quraysh and Thaqif: these are used for tribes more often, or if they are taken as names of tribes, it is permissible and good. The lam in li-Ilafi is for causation, and the prepositional phrase is, according to al-Khalil, related to the verb in "li-ya'budu". 

The fa' is because of the conditional sense in the statement, since the meaning is that the blessings of Allah the Exalted are not limited; so if they do not worship Him for all His other blessings, then let them worship Him for this great blessing. And since it is not in the response of an actual condition, it is in reality superfluous, so there is no prohibition on placing the object of what follows it before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 106, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their journeys of winter and summer﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the covenant of Quraysh" (ilaf Quraysh), and "rihlata" (journey) is the direct object of "ilafihim" (their covenant), on the assumption that it derives from al-ulfah (familiarity, affection). But if it derives from al-mu'alafah in the sense of al-mu'ahadah (covenant, pact), then it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid); that is, "their covenant concerning, or for the sake of, the journey..." etc. The unrestricted mention of "ilaf" followed by the substitution of the restricted term for it serves to magnify it. It is related from al-Akhfash that the preposition is connected to an implied verb; that is: "We did what We did, namely the destruction of the People of the Elephant, for the covenant of Quraysh."

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said likewise, except that they estimated the verb from the context: "Are you amazed?" as if it were said: "Are you amazed at the covenant of Quraysh, the journey of winter and summer, and their abandonment of the worship of God, exalted is He, who honoured them, provided for them and granted them security? Therefore they were commanded to worship their Lord, who bestowed upon them provision and security," so He followed it and linked it with the resultative fa' (fa' al-tafriT).

Also from al-Akhfash: it is connected to "ja'alahum" (He made them), as in "like chewed-up stalks" (ka-'asf) in the surah before it, and the Qur'an as a whole is like a single surah; therefore separation by the basmalah does no harm, contrary to a group of scholars.

The meaning: Glorified is He, He destroyed those from Abyssinia who intended them, and did not give them power over them, so that they would remain in what they were upon of "their journeys of winter and summer." Or, mighty and majestic is He, He destroyed those who intended them so that people would take heed and no one would dare against them, and their journey would be fully secure. This does not contradict that their destruction was for their disbelief in disrespecting the House, because it is permissible to give the cause as two matters; each of them is not a true (haqiqi) cause, so multiplicity is not impossible.

Many have said: the lam is for consequence (al-'aqibah), and Quraysh had two journeys: a journey in winter to Yemen, and a journey in summer to Busra in the land of Syria, as related from Ibn 'Abbas. In their two journeys they were secure, because they were the people of the Sacred Precinct of God, the Exalted, and the custodians of His Mighty House; so no one would attack them, while people were snatched away or plundered. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that they used to travel in summer to al-Ta'if, where there is water and shade, and travel in winter to Makkah for trade and their other needs. The word "journey" is given in the singular, although the intended meaning is the two journeys of winter and summer, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity and making the meaning clear. A parallel to it is his saying:

"O dove of the valley between the two valleys, sing,"

where he did not say "bottoms of the two valleys" (batnay). And his saying:

"Eat from a part of your bellies, so that you may abstain; for your time is a lean time."

where he did not say "bellies" (butun) in the plural for this reason. Sibawayh's saying that this is not permitted except in poetic necessity is open to question. Al-Naqqash said: they had four journeys, and Ibn 'Atiyyah objected that this is a rejected view. In al-Bahr: it should not be rejected, for the people of the ilaf were four brothers, and they are: the sons of 'Abd Manaf: Hashim, who had an agreement with the king of Syria, from whom he took horses and so was secure in his trade to Syria; 'Abd Shams, who had an agreement with Abyssinia; al-Muttalib, with Yemen; and Nawfal, with Persia. These were called "the traders" (al-mutta-jirin), so Quraysh's trade passed through the horses of these brothers and was not attacked.

Al-Azhari said: the ilaf is similar to a contract of protection (ijarah bi-al-khifarah), so if that is the case, it is permissible that they had four journeys, according to these places in which trade was under the protection of these four. Thus "rihlah" here is a noun of genus that suits one or many. About these brothers the poet says:

"O man who changes his saddle-bag, why did you not stop with the family of 'Abd Manaf?

Those who take the pact from its horizons, and those who set out on the journey of ilaf;

those who give (the rish, provision of wealth), though there is none who gives, and those who say 'come here' to the guests;

and those who mix their rich with their poor until the poor among them becomes like the sufficient."

End of quotation. In it there is a contradiction with what we previously quoted from al-Harawi. Moreover, the intention of the four journeys mentioned is not clearly apparent, as is not hidden.

Ibn 'Amir read "li-ilaf Quraysh" without a ya'. The reasoning for this is what has passed. The Seven did not differ in reading "ilafihim" with the ya', unlike the first. Nevertheless, the first was written in the 'Uthmanic codices with a ya', and the second was written without a ya', as al-Samin said, and he took this as one of the proofs that readers are bound by transmission (riwayah) by hearing, not by the script of the codex. It has been mentioned as an explanation of this that the first was written according to the original form, and the second was left out relying on the first; but this, as you see, is weak, so reflect.

It is related from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, that he recited with two hamzahs in both, the second being silent; this is anomalous, although it is the original form, and it seems they replaced the hamzah that is the first radical of the word because of the heaviness of two hamzahs together. Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Naqqar related from 'Asim: "i'ilafihim" with two kasra'd hamzahs followed by a silent ya' arising from the vowel of the second hamzah when it was lengthened; but the correct view is that he retracted from reciting with two hamzahs and that he recited like the majority.

Abu Ja'far, as related by al-Zamakhshari, recited "li-ilf Quraysh", and as related by Ibn 'Atiyyah, he recited "ilfihim". It is also reported from 'Ikrimah and Ibn Kathir, and they recited the verse:

"You claim that your brothers are Quraysh, that they have ilf (affection), and you have no ilaf (covenant)."

From Abu Ja'far also, and Ibn 'Amir: "ilafihim" in the pattern fi'al. From Abu Ja'far also: "li-yilaf", with a silent ya' after the lam, and he explained it by saying that when he changed the second to a ya', he deleted the first by a deletion not following analogy.

From 'Ikrimah: "li-ta'laf Quraysh", in the form of the present tense subjunctive with an implied "an" after the lam, and Quraysh in the nominative as subject; and also from him: "li-ta'lif", in the imperative; and from him and from Hilal ibn Fityan, with a fatha on the lam of the imperative. The apparent view is that "ilafahum" in all of these is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); and I have not seen anyone who addressed this. Abu al-Sammal recited "ruhlah" with a damma on the ra'; and in that case it means the direction to which one travels. As for the ra' with a kasra, it is a verbal noun, as stated explicitly in al-Bahr.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 106, verses 3–4:

﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ — that is the Ka'bah, which was protected from the companions of the Elephant (Ashab al-Fil).

And it is related from Umar that he led the people in prayer at Makkah by the Ka'bah, and when he recited "So let them worship the Lord of this House," he began to point with his finger toward it, while he was in prayer, between the hands of Allah the Exalted.

﴿Who has fed them﴾ — by means of those two journeys which they were able to make because they were neighbours of Him, ﴿against hunger﴾, a severe hunger in which they had been before them. It has also been said that what is meant is the famine in which they ate carrion and bones.

﴿And has secured them from fear﴾ — a great fear whose magnitude cannot be measured, namely the fear of the companions of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched away in their land and during their travels, or the fear of leprosy; as Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn Abbas. Thus they are not afflicted in their land, as a favour from Him, the Exalted, such as plague.

And also from him (Ibn Abbas): he said, "He fed them against hunger through the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he said: ﴿And provide for them from the fruits﴾, and ﴿and has secured them from fear﴾, when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾."

As for "min" (from), it has been said that it is causal (ta'liliyyah), meaning: He bestowed favour upon them and fed them in order to remove hunger from them. Either a noun is supposed to be elided so that the soundness of the causal sense becomes apparent, or it is said that hunger is an inciting cause and no elision is needed. It has also been said that it is partitive (badaliyyah), like it in His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾. Al-Kirmani, in Gharaib al-Tafsir, related that it was said regarding His, the Exalted's, words ﴿and has secured them from fear﴾ that the caliphate would only be among them; and this is utterly false, as is not hidden. Al-Musayyibi related from Nafi' a reading "min khawfin" with the nun concealed before the kha', and this is attributed to Sibawayh; and likewise its concealment before the 'ayn, as in "min 'ala" for example. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
